title: Peddi Made ₹345 Crore in a Week. The Conversation It Started About Janhvi Kapoor Won't Cost a Thing.
excerpt: Ram Charan delivered the biggest Telugu opener of 2026 — and then the internet noticed what his film did with its leading lady, and the director had to cut scenes.
body:
**Peddi** arrived on June 4 like a lorry with no brakes. **Ram Charan** — shredded, intense, looking like he'd been carved out of granite by someone who studied anatomy at a temple — opened the film at ₹69 crore net in India. By midnight, the worldwide gross had crossed ₹100 crore. By the end of its first week, the **Buchi Babu Sana** sports drama had piled up ₹345 crore worldwide, making it the biggest Telugu opener of 2026 and one of the top five Indian films of the year.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=sF2dj7ycZvA</youtube>

And then the conversation shifted.

It didn't shift to the cinematography, which is sweeping and gorgeous. It didn't shift to the score or to Ram Charan's physical transformation — though both deserve their flowers. It shifted to **Janhvi Kapoor**, and specifically to what the film chose to do with her.

> "The heroine deserved a character. Instead she got a string of vulgar, degrading, objectifying scenes stitched together and called a role." — viewer on social media

The backlash was swift and specific. Viewers flagged sequences where Janhvi's character, Achiyamma, was shot through a lens that treated her body as set decoration rather than a person with agency. One scene — where a goon undresses her publicly while another character watches and laughs — drew particular fury. Reddit threads went nuclear. The word "objectifying" trended in Telugu-language Twitter for two consecutive days.

Director Buchi Babu Sana, to his credit, didn't hide. He issued a public apology within days.

> "A few shots turned misleading. We have taken corrective measures to remove them." — Buchi Babu Sana, speaking to SCREEN

The scenes were cut from prints still running in cinemas — a rare admission that a ₹345 crore film got something fundamentally wrong on the way to getting almost everything else right.

**Jagapathi Babu**, who plays a key supporting role, defended Janhvi directly at the film's Thank You meet in Hyderabad. "Please don't target the actor," he said. "She did what the director asked her to do. When an actor signs on and trusts a director's vision, they follow that vision." He added, with the seasoned diplomacy of a veteran who's navigated industry cycles before: "To those who wrote bad reviews — I thank you even more. You have unknowingly helped us."

He might be right about that last part. The controversy hasn't slowed the film's collection much. Ram Charan's performance — raw, committed, a genuine transformation from the sleeker star the audience knows — has carried the film through the noise. **Allu Arjun** praised his cousin publicly, calling it a "gritty, raw performance" with "extraordinary body transformation and graceful dance moves."

But the real story is in the numbers that didn't work. Peddi was launched as a pan-India film with a massive Hindi marketing push, including a star-studded launch event in Bhopal with **Boman Irani** and **Divyenndu** in the ensemble. The result? The Hindi version collected barely ₹15 crore net — less than 5% of the film's total haul. North India simply didn't show up. Telugu audiences drove the engine, powering the domestic gross to ₹230 crore while overseas markets added another layer. In North America, Peddi crossed **$5 million** in its first week, entering the elite $3M club in just four days — joining only OG and MSVP in the last 18 months.

For the Indian diaspora, especially NRIs who follow Telugu cinema, Peddi remains a must-see in the corrected prints now playing in US, UK, and Canadian theatres. The controversial scenes have been removed. What's left is a muscular sports drama with a lead performance that has genuine award-season potential.

But the film leaves a complicated taste. Here is a ₹345 crore commercial juggernaut that also became a national conversation about the male gaze in Indian cinema. The director apologised. The scenes were cut. Janhvi has said nothing publicly — and maybe that's the smartest move of all. In an industry that routinely asks its women to smile through worse, her silence reads less like complicity and more like a refusal to do the studio's PR cleanup for them.

Ram Charan built a god on screen. The film made a fortune. But the argument it started — about what Indian blockbusters owe the women standing next to their leading men — is worth more than any opening weekend.
